A convex objective and a concave eyepiece, separated by the difference of their focal lengths
q.explanation: A Galilean telescope has a plus objective and a minus eyepiece, separated by the difference of their focal lengths. It gives an erect, magnified, virtual image and is compact enough to mount on spectacles. Two convex lenses separated by the sum of their focal lengths make an astronomical telescope, which gives an inverted image.

q.stem: A Galilean telescope has a +10 D objective and a -30 D eyepiece. What are its magnification and tube length?
q.explanation: M = Fe/Fo = 30/10 = x3 (magnitude). Tube length = fo - |fe| = 10 cm - 3.33 cm = 6.67 cm. Adding the focal lengths (13.3 cm) gives the astronomical arrangement. x0.33 inverts the ratio.

q.stem: A Galilean telescope uses a +8 D objective and a -20 D eyepiece. What are its magnification and lens separation?
q.explanation: M = 20/8 = x2.5. The objective focal length is 12.5 cm and the eyepiece focal length is 5 cm, so the separation is 12.5 - 5 = 7.5 cm. 17.5 cm adds the focal lengths, and x0.4 inverts the ratio.

q.stem: Which of the following is NOT a limitation of optical magnifying low vision aids?
options: Field of view decreases as magnification increases
The object must be held close to the eye
Higher magnification increases the depth of field
q.explanation: Magnification reduces both depth of focus and depth of field. It does not increase them. The other options are genuine limitations: a narrow field makes rapid scanning difficult, the working distance is critical, and objects must be held close.

q.stem: Which low vision aid shows an enlarged image of the text on a screen?
q.explanation: CCTV is a projection system that presents an enlarged image on a screen. Telescopes and convex magnifiers give angular magnification through lenses.

q.stem: In a direct ophthalmoscope, why is the real image of the bulb formed just below the sight-hole rather than in line with it?
options: To increase the magnification of the fundus image
To make the field of view evenly illuminated
So that the corneal reflection of the light lies outside the observer's visual axis
To allow the correcting lenses to be placed closer to the patient
q.explanation: Placing the bulb image just beneath the aperture keeps the bright corneal reflex out of the observer's line of sight. The trade-off is that the illuminated field is uneven, so it does not improve the evenness of illumination, and it has nothing to do with magnification or the lens wheel.

q.stem: Compared with an emmetropic eye, how does the field of view of the direct ophthalmoscope change when examining a myopic and a hypermetropic patient?
options: Larger in myopia, smaller in hypermetropia
Smaller in myopia, larger in hypermetropia
Unchanged; it depends only on the observer's pupil
q.explanation: With the direct ophthalmoscope the field is restricted in myopia and widened in hypermetropia. Combined with the larger image in myopia, this is why a myopic fundus is harder to survey. Pupil size and the sight-hole also limit the field, but refractive state still matters.

q.stem: Which manoeuvre most increases the field of view during direct ophthalmoscopy?
options: Moving further away from the patient to see more of the fundus
Dilating the patient's pupil and getting as close as possible to the eye
Racking up a stronger plus lens
q.explanation: The field of view widens considerably with a dilated pupil and grows as the observer-patient distance shrinks, so the examiner should get as close as possible. Moving away reduces the field; filters and lens powers do not enlarge it.

q.stem: With the direct ophthalmoscope, how does the size of the observer's retinal image of the fundus vary with the patient's refractive state?
options: Larger in hypermetropia and smaller in myopia
The same in all refractive states once a correcting lens is used
Larger in both myopia and hypermetropia
Smaller in hypermetropia and larger in myopia than in emmetropia
q.explanation: The image is magnified more in myopia and less in hypermetropia. A correcting lens reduces this discrepancy but does not remove it completely, so 'the same in all states' is wrong.

q.stem: An emmetropic observer, without accommodating, uses a direct ophthalmoscope on a patient with 4 D of uncorrected myopia. What happens and what is needed?
options: Diverging light focuses behind the observer's retina; a +4 D lens is needed
Converging light focuses in front of the observer's retina; a -4 D lens is needed
Parallel light reaches the observer; no lens is needed
Converging light; the observer can clear it by accommodating 4 D
q.explanation: Light leaving a myopic eye converges, so it focuses in front of the observer's retina and the image is blurred. A concave lens equal to the vergence (about -4 D) makes it parallel. Accommodation adds plus power and only makes a converging beam worse; that strategy works only for hypermetropic patients.

q.stem: An emmetropic observer views the fundus of a +3 D hypermetropic patient with a direct ophthalmoscope. Without a correcting lens, how can the observer get a clear view?
options: By relaxing accommodation, because the emerging light is convergent
No view is possible without a -3 D lens
By accommodating about 3 D, because the emerging light is divergent
By moving further away from the patient
q.explanation: Light leaving a hypermetropic eye diverges. The emmetropic observer can bring it to a focus either by accommodating or by racking up a convex lens of about +3 D. A minus lens would add more divergence.

q.stem: Why is it difficult to examine a highly myopic fundus with the direct ophthalmoscope?
options: The image is small and the field wide, so detail is lost
The fundus cannot be focused with any lens in the instrument
Total internal reflection at the cornea blocks the view
The image is large and the field of view small, so little of the fundus is seen at once
q.explanation: In myopia the direct ophthalmoscope gives a large image with a reduced field, and in axial myopia the globe itself is bigger. The posterior pole is often seen best with the patient's own glasses left on. A small image with a wide field is what you get in hypermetropia.

q.stem: Why does the optic disc look oval when a highly astigmatic eye is viewed through a direct ophthalmoscope?
options: The disc really is oval in all astigmatic eyes
The red-free filter distorts the image
The observer's own astigmatism is always the cause
The two principal meridians magnify differently and the instrument has only spherical lenses
q.explanation: The ophthalmoscope's lens wheel contains spheres only, so only one meridian can be focused at a time. The different dioptric power in the two principal meridians also gives different magnifications, so the disc looks distorted and oval.

q.stem: A -3.00 D myopic observer takes off their glasses to examine a +5.00 D hypermetropic patient with a direct ophthalmoscope. Ignoring vertex distances, which ophthalmoscope lens should give a clear view?
q.explanation: The lens needed is the algebraic sum of the two refractive errors: +5.00 + (-3.00) = +2.00 D. +8.00 D comes from adding the sizes and ignoring the observer's minus sign. -2.00 D is the right size with the wrong sign.

q.stem: A +2.00 D hypermetropic observer, without glasses or accommodation, examines a -6.00 D myopic patient with a direct ophthalmoscope. Ignoring vertex distances, which lens should be dialled?
q.explanation: Add the two errors algebraically: -6.00 + (+2.00) = -4.00 D. -8.00 D treats the observer's plus as minus. -6.00 D corrects only the patient and ignores the observer's own error.

q.stem: An ametropic examiner keeps their spectacles on while using the direct ophthalmoscope. What is the main drawback?
options: Magnification drops to roughly a quarter
The field of view is reduced because the examiner cannot get as close to the patient
The correcting lenses in the instrument stop working
q.explanation: Glasses push the examiner further from the patient's eye, and the field of view shrinks as that distance grows. Orientation and the lens wheel are not affected.

q.stem: Taking the patient's emmetropic eye as +60 D, what is the magnification of the direct ophthalmoscope?
q.explanation: The patient's eye acts as a simple magnifier (a loupe), so M = F/4 = 60/4 = 15. x4 confuses the formula's divisor (4, from the 25 cm near-point reference) with the answer. x3 is the angular magnification of a +20 D indirect lens.

q.stem: A patient's eye has a total power of +64 D. Using M = F/4, what is the expected magnification with the direct ophthalmoscope?
q.explanation: M = F/4 = 64/4 = 16. x15 is the textbook figure for a +60 D eye. x256 comes from multiplying instead of dividing, and x4.9 is roughly 64/13, which mixes in the indirect-lens formula.

q.stem: Why does a red-free filter on the direct ophthalmoscope help in diabetic retinopathy?
options: It increases the magnification to x30
It allows the peripheral retina to be seen
Micro-aneurysms show up as black dots against a green background
q.explanation: With the red-free (green) filter, red structures such as micro-aneurysms look dark against a green background and are easier to spot. Together with the x15 magnification, this makes the direct ophthalmoscope well suited to retinopathy screening. The filter changes neither magnification nor field.

q.stem: Which setting allows the direct ophthalmoscope to be used as an illuminated loupe to inspect lens opacities?
options: The 0 D lens with the observer standing at 1 m
The red-free filter with the -20 D lens
q.explanation: With the +10 D lens racked up, the instrument becomes a self-illuminating magnifier for the anterior segment, so lens opacities can be inspected directly.

q.stem: In binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy of an emmetropic eye, where is the image of the fundus and what is its orientation?
options: A virtual erect image behind the patient's eye
A real image at the second principal focus of the condensing lens, inverted both vertically and laterally
A real image at the patient's pupil, inverted vertically only
A virtual image at the observer's near point, erect
q.explanation: The condensing lens forms a real image between itself and the observer, at its second focal point for an emmetropic eye. The image is inverted both vertically and laterally. Virtual erect images belong to the direct ophthalmoscope and the Hruby lens.

q.stem: For an emmetropic patient, about how far from a +13 D condensing lens is the aerial image formed?
options: About 13 cm on the observer's side
About 7.7 cm on the patient's side
About 5 cm on the observer's side
About 7.7 cm on the observer's side
q.explanation: Light leaving an emmetropic eye is parallel, so the image lies at the second principal focus: f = 1/13 m = 0.077 m, roughly 8 cm towards the observer. 13 cm confuses dioptres with centimetres, and 5 cm is the focal length of a +20 D lens. The image is real, so it forms on the observer's side.

q.stem: Which factors limit the field of view (as opposed to the field of illumination) in indirect ophthalmoscopy?
options: The patient's pupil size and refractive state
The observer's pupil size and the diameter of the condensing lens
The distance between the observer and the patient's lens only
q.explanation: The field of view depends on the observer's pupil and on the aperture of the condensing lens: larger lenses give a larger field. The patient's pupil and refractive state govern the field of illumination. Dilating the observer's pupil is impractical because it adds aberrations and removes accommodation.

q.stem: Why are condensing lenses for indirect ophthalmoscopy made with aspheric surfaces?
options: To increase the dioptric power without increasing thickness
q.explanation: Strong condensing lenses would suffer significant aberrations if they were spherical. Aspheric surfaces reduce these. The image stays inverted whatever the surface form.

q.stem: Taking the nodal point to retina distance as 15 mm, what is the approximate linear magnification of the fundus image with a +20 D condensing lens?
q.explanation: Linear magnification = focal length of the condensing lens / nodal point to retina distance. f = 1/20 m = 50 mm, and 50/15 = 3.3. x5 is the value for a +13 D lens (75/15). x1.3 comes from using 20 mm as the focal length.

q.stem: Taking the eye as +60 D, what is the approximate angular magnification of the indirect image with a +13 D condensing lens?
q.explanation: Angular magnification = power of the eye / power of the condensing lens = 60/13 = 4.6, i.e. about x5. x3 is the value for a +20 D lens, and x0.22 is the ratio taken upside down. Stronger condensing lenses give less magnification.

q.stem: An examiner swaps a +20 D condensing lens for a +30 D lens. Taking the eye as +60 D, what is the new angular magnification, and what happens to the image?
options: x2; the image is smaller (and the field wider)
q.explanation: 60/30 = 2, compared with 60/20 = 3 for the +20 D lens. A stronger condensing lens gives a smaller image. Magnification is inversely related to lens power.

q.stem: In indirect ophthalmoscopy of a myopic eye, where is the aerial image formed relative to the condensing lens's second principal focus, and what happens to its size as the lens is moved away from the eye?
options: Inside the focus; the image gets larger
Outside the focus; the image gets larger
Inside the focus; the image gets smaller
At the focus; the size does not change
q.explanation: Convergent light from a myopic eye is brought to a focus before the second principal focus. As the lens is withdrawn the image enlarges in myopia and shrinks in hypermetropia, and examiners can use this to judge refractive state. Only in emmetropia does the image sit exactly at the focus.

q.section: The Relative Merits of the Direct and Indirect Ophthalmoscope
q.stem: Which feature makes the indirect ophthalmoscope the preferred instrument during retinal detachment surgery?
options: It is used at a distance, so a sterile operative field can be kept
It gives the highest magnification of any ophthalmoscope
q.explanation: Because the indirect ophthalmoscope is used at arm's length, the surgeon can keep a sterile field. It also gives bright illumination and a wide field, and it can deliver laser. Its magnification is lower than the direct instrument's and its image is inverted.

q.section: The Relative Merits of the Direct and Indirect Ophthalmoscope
q.stem: Which statement about the direct and indirect ophthalmoscopes is correct?
options: The direct ophthalmoscope is best for the retinal periphery
Laser cannot be delivered through an indirect ophthalmoscope
The indirect ophthalmoscope is smaller and lighter
The indirect instrument copes better with media opacities because of its stronger light source
q.explanation: Indirect ophthalmoscopes are bigger, with more powerful lights, and this helps when the media are hazy. Their bright illumination and wide field make them the choice for the periphery and for detachments, and laser photocoagulation can be delivered through them.

q.stem: In the reflex stage of retinoscopy, where is the image of the illuminated retina formed?
options: At the anterior focal point of the patient's eye
q.explanation: The illuminated fundus is imaged at the patient's far point. Neutralisation happens when that far point coincides with the observer's nodal point (the sight-hole).

q.stem: With a modern streak retinoscope, which sleeve position gives the 'plane mirror' effect with much brighter illumination than the lowest position?
options: The highest position, where a true concave mirror effect is obtained
The exact middle of the sleeve travel, where the light is collimated
Just below the lowest position, so the instrument acts like a concave mirror whose focal length slightly exceeds the working distance
Any position, because brightness does not depend on the sleeve
q.explanation: Moving the condensing lens a short way from its lowest position keeps the plane mirror effect (the light still behaves as diverging at the patient) and makes the beam brighter. This helps with small pupils and hazy media. The highest position gives the concave mirror effect, which reverses the reflex movement.

q.stem: A patient has -1.00 D myopia. With no lens in place, a retinoscopist works at 67 cm. What reflex is seen?
options: No reflex because the far point is behind the eye
q.explanation: The working distance is 1/0.67 = 1.50 D. Myopia smaller than the dioptric value of the working distance still gives a 'with' movement. The far point (1 m) lies beyond the observer, not at them.

q.stem: A patient has -2.50 D myopia. Retinoscopy is done at 67 cm with no lens. What will the reflex do?
q.explanation: The working distance equals 1.50 D. The myopia (2.50 D) exceeds this, so the far point (40 cm) lies between patient and observer and the reflex moves against. Neutral would need 1.50 D of myopia.

q.stem: Working at 67 cm, a retinoscopist neutralises the reflex with a +4.00 DS lens. What is the patient's refractive error?
q.explanation: Take off the working distance allowance: 1/0.67 = 1.50 D, so +4.00 - 1.50 = +2.50 D. +5.50 comes from adding the allowance instead of subtracting it. +3.00 uses the 1 m allowance (1.00 D).

q.stem: Working at 1 m, retinoscopy neutralises with -2.00 DS. What is the refractive error?
q.explanation: For a 1 m working distance the allowance is -1.00 D, so -2.00 + (-1.00) = -3.00 D. -1.00 comes from subtracting the allowance the wrong way. -3.50 applies the 67 cm allowance.

q.stem: A retinoscopist working at 50 cm neutralises the reflex with +1.00 DS. What is the patient's refractive error?
q.explanation: A 50 cm working distance corresponds to 2.00 D, so subtract 2.00 D: +1.00 - 2.00 = -1.00 D. +3.00 comes from adding the allowance. +1.00 ignores the working distance altogether. So the eye is actually myopic even though a plus lens neutralised it.

q.stem: As the neutral point is approached during retinoscopy, how does the reflex behave?
options: It moves more slowly and dims
It moves faster and becomes brighter, filling the pupil at neutral
It changes from red to green
It always switches suddenly from 'with' to 'against' without speeding up
q.explanation: The reflex speeds up as reversal approaches. At neutral, the far point is at the observer's nodal point, the movement is infinitely fast, and the pupil appears filled with a diffuse bright red glow.

q.stem: When a Placido disc is reflected from an astigmatic cornea, where do the rings lie closer together?
q.explanation: A shorter radius of curvature gives a smaller reflected image, so the rings crowd together in the steeper meridian. The same principle is used in computerised videokeratography and to guide suturing during surgery.

q.stem: Why is a convex lens mounted in the central aperture of a Placido disc?
options: To project the rings onto the cornea
To neutralise the patient's refractive error
To magnify the reflected image and relieve the examiner's need to accommodate
To double the image for measurement
q.explanation: The examiner looks through the central hole at the corneal reflection of the rings. A convex lens there magnifies the image and saves the examiner from accommodating. Image doubling is a keratometer feature.

q.stem: Taking the keratometric index as 1.3375, what corneal power corresponds to an anterior radius of 7.5 mm?
q.explanation: D = (n2 - n1)/r = (1.3375 - 1)/0.0075 = 0.3375/0.0075 = 45.00 D. 43.27 D is the value for 7.8 mm. 4.50 D comes from putting r in cm rather than metres.

q.stem: Using a refractive index of 1.3375, what is the anterior corneal radius of curvature if the keratometer reads 44.00 D?
q.explanation: r = (n2 - n1)/D = 0.3375/44 = 0.00767 m = 7.67 mm. 7.80 mm corresponds to about 43.27 D and 7.50 mm to 45.00 D.

q.stem: Keratometry gives radii of 7.50 mm horizontally and 7.80 mm vertically. Using an index of 1.3375, about how much corneal astigmatism is present?
q.explanation: Horizontal: 0.3375/0.0075 = 45.00 D. Vertical: 0.3375/0.0078 = 43.27 D. The difference is 1.73 D, about 1.75 D, with the horizontal meridian steeper (against-the-rule). 0.30 is just the difference in radii in mm, not dioptres.

q.stem: In keratometry the cornea acts as a convex mirror and the image lies close to its focal point, so I/O = r/(2u). With u = 75 mm, object size O = 60 mm and measured image size I = 3 mm, what is the corneal radius?
q.explanation: Rearranging gives r = 2u x I/O = 2 x 75 x 3/60 = 7.5 mm. 3.75 mm forgets the factor of 2 (taking v = r rather than r/2), and 15 mm doubles twice.

q.stem: How do the von Helmholtz and Javal-Schiøtz keratometers differ in what they keep fixed?
options: Von Helmholtz fixes image size; Javal-Schiøtz fixes object size
Von Helmholtz fixes object size and varies image size; Javal-Schiøtz fixes image size and varies object size
Both fix the image size and vary the viewing distance
q.explanation: Both use r = 2u(I/O) with u held constant. Von Helmholtz keeps the mire separation (O) fixed and measures I with doubling plates. Javal-Schiøtz keeps the doubled image size fixed and moves the mires to change O.

q.stem: Why do keratometers double the image of the mires?
options: To measure both corneal surfaces at once
To compensate for the patient's refractive error
So that small eye movements move both images together and they can still be aligned
q.explanation: Natural eye movements make a single image 'dance', which makes it hard to measure. When the image is doubled, both copies move together, and the reading is taken by bringing their edges into contact. Von Helmholtz uses tilting glass plates for this; Javal-Schiøtz uses a Wollaston prism.

q.stem: Which optical component doubles the image in the Javal-Schiøtz keratometer?
options: A Wollaston prism in the viewing telescope
q.explanation: Javal-Schiøtz uses a Wollaston prism in the telescope. Rotating inclined glass plates are the von Helmholtz method. Porro prisms erect the image in microscopes.

q.stem: With a Javal-Schiøtz keratometer, the mire images are aligned in one meridian. Rotated 90 degrees, the images overlap by 2 steps. How much corneal astigmatism is there?
q.explanation: Each step of the stepped mire represents 1 D of corneal power, so an overlap of 2 steps means 2.00 D of astigmatism between the principal meridians.

q.stem: Which method of corneal topography projects a grid onto the fluorescein-stained tear film and can still map an irregular or poorly reflecting surface extending onto the sclera?
q.explanation: Raster photogrammetry casts a grid 'like a net over a hill' and calculates height above a reference plane. It works even on irregular, poorly reflecting surfaces and onto the sclera. CVK depends on a Placido image reflected from a 5-6 mm zone.

q.stem: In a computerised videokeratography map, what does a single colour represent?
q.explanation: CVK digitises the reflected Placido rings and shows them as a colour-coded contour map in which points of the same dioptric power share a colour. Its uses include astigmatism measurement, contact lens fitting, refractive surgery and keratoconus.

q.stem: In a compound microscope, where is the object placed and what is the final image without erecting prisms?
options: Inside the objective's focal length; the final image is erect
Just outside the objective's anterior focal point; the final image is inverted vertically and horizontally
At the eyepiece's focal point; the final image is erect
At twice the objective's focal length; the image is inverted vertically only
q.explanation: The objective forms a real, inverted, magnified intermediate image at or near the eyepiece focal point, and the eyepiece then magnifies it further. The final image is inverted in both meridians, so Porro prisms are added to erect it and to shorten the instrument.

q.stem: Which zoom system keeps the object-lens distance constant and is preferred for the operating microscope?
options: Uncompensated zoom, with a single movable concave lens
Compensated zoom, with several movable lenses
q.explanation: In an uncompensated zoom, a single movable concave lens changes magnification but also shifts the image position. A compensated system moves several lenses and keeps the object-lens distance constant, which is why it suits the operating microscope.

q.stem: What allows the magnification of most slit-lamp microscopes to be changed?
options: A bank of Galilean telescopes of different powers
A single movable concave lens with no other optics
q.explanation: Most slit lamps contain a turret of Galilean telescopes that can be switched to change magnification. Prisms in the shortened tubes erect the image. Slit width affects illumination, not magnification.

q.stem: Which slit-lamp technique is used to view the corneal endothelium, with the patient's gaze bisecting the angle between the illumination and observation axes?
q.explanation: Specular reflection shows the corneal endothelium and anterior lens capsule. The arm positions are set so that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

q.stem: A slit beam directed at the temporal limbus makes the whole limbus glow, with total internal reflection carrying light within the cornea. Which technique is this?
q.explanation: In sclerotic scatter, the light bounces between the corneal surfaces and lights up the limbus all the way round; the slit lamp must be decentred to do it. In lateral illumination, light is directed beside a lesion so that the lesion glows.

q.stem: Areas of iris atrophy are best seen by light reflected back from the fundus/choroid. What is this technique called?
q.explanation: Retro-illumination lights a structure from behind using light reflected off a deeper structure. Transillumination defects in the iris are the classic example.

q.stem: Which slit-lamp technique is most useful for translucent lesions such as iris nodules, where light directed just beside the lesion makes it glow from within?
q.explanation: Lateral illumination puts the beam just to the side of the lesion so that some light enters it and lights it internally. This works well for translucent corneal opacities and iris nodules.

q.stem: Why do blue or green (red-free) filters help when examining the vitreous with the slit lamp?
options: Long wavelengths penetrate the vitreous better
Fluorescein in the vitreous glows under these filters
Short wavelengths scatter more from the gel, and less light returns from the choroid, so the background is darker
q.explanation: Vitreous structure becomes visible by scattering, which is greater for short wavelengths. Little short-wavelength light comes back from the choroid, so the dark background makes structures such as a detached posterior hyaloid easier to see. The cobalt blue filter is used mainly for applanation tonometry.

q.stem: What is the Hruby lens, and what image does it form?
options: A +90 D biconvex lens forming a real, inverted image
A -58.6 D lens forming a real, inverted, magnified image
A high-power convex contact lens forming a real image inside a glass sphere
A -58.6 D plano-concave lens forming a virtual, erect, diminished image within the slit lamp's focal range
q.explanation: The Hruby lens is held just in front of the eye with its concave face towards the cornea. It cancels roughly the eye's power, giving a virtual, erect, diminished image near the pupil plane that the slit lamp can focus on. 90 D and 78 D lenses give real inverted images, as does the panfunduscope.

q.stem: Why are +90 D and +78 D lenses used for slit-lamp indirect ophthalmoscopy instead of +20 D lenses?
options: They give a larger image than a +20 D lens
They are better for the far retinal periphery
Their short focal length brings the real image within the slit-lamp microscope's focal range
q.explanation: High-power condensing lenses shorten the light path so the aerial image falls within the slit lamp's range. They make the image smaller, but the microscope's magnification more than makes up for this. They are best for the posterior pole, less so for the periphery.

q.stem: Which fundus lens is a high-power convex contact lens that forms a real, inverted image inside a spherical glass element and gives a field of about 120 degrees?
q.explanation: The panfunduscope acts as a condensing lens sitting on the cornea, so its field is very wide (about 120 degrees, to the equator). The Goldmann fundus lens and the Hruby lens work by negative power and give virtual erect images.

q.stem: When viewing the fundus with a slit-lamp lens, how is the corneal reflection kept out of the microscope?
options: By using the widest possible slit
By using the cobalt blue filter
By tilting the illumination column so its axis lies below the viewing axis
By moving the lens away until the image disappears
q.explanation: Reflections from the cornea degrade the view when the illuminating and viewing paths overlap at the cornea. Tilting the light column separates them.

q.stem: What is the commonest use of specular microscopy, and how is it viewed?
options: Mapping corneal curvature; viewed with both eyes
Assessing the endothelium of donor corneas; viewed with one eye only
Imaging the retinal nerve fibre layer; viewed monocularly
q.explanation: Specular microscopy shows the endothelial mosaic because cell bodies and intercellular borders reflect differently. The angle between the illumination and observation axes is critical, so the reflection is seen with only one eye.

q.stem: Why is the Goldmann tonometer designed to flatten a circle of cornea 3.06 mm in diameter?
options: At this diameter corneal rigidity and tear-film surface tension cancel, so the applied force is proportional to IOP
It is the diameter of the pupil in normal light
It gives the largest possible displacement of aqueous
It matches the diameter of the endothelial cells
q.explanation: At 3.06 mm the outward corneal rigidity (R) and the inward pull of tear surface tension (S) balance, so W is proportional to P. The volume displaced is also tiny, so the IOP is barely changed by the measurement.

q.stem: What does the operator see through the Goldmann prism when the reading is correct?
options: Two semicircles whose outer edges touch
Two fluorescein semicircles whose inner edges just touch
q.explanation: The two prisms, mounted base to base in opposite directions, split the contact ring into two laterally displaced half-rings. The dial is turned until their inner edges meet.

q.stem: A patient with 8 D of with-the-rule corneal astigmatism reads 18 mmHg by Goldmann tonometry with the prism at the horizontal mark. What is the approximate true IOP?
q.explanation: With-the-rule astigmatism makes the reading about 1 mmHg too low per 4 D. 8 D gives about 2 mmHg underestimation, so the true IOP is about 18 + 2 = 20 mmHg. 16 applies the correction in the wrong direction. 26 adds 1 mmHg per dioptre.

q.stem: With 4 D of against-the-rule corneal astigmatism, Goldmann tonometry reads 21 mmHg. What is the approximate true IOP?
q.explanation: Against-the-rule astigmatism makes the reading about 1 mmHg too high per 4 D, so 21 - 1 = 20 mmHg. 22 corrects the wrong way. 17 subtracts the full 4 D as if it were mmHg.

q.stem: How should the Goldmann prism be set for a patient with significant regular corneal astigmatism?
options: Align the white mark with the axis of the plus cylinder
Rotate the prism so the red 43-degree mark lines up with the axis of the minus cylinder
Leave it at horizontal; astigmatism has no effect
Rotate it 90 degrees to the steepest meridian
q.explanation: Taking the measurement 43 degrees from the flatter meridian averages out the error. In practice the red (A) mark is placed at the minus-cylinder axis. Small or oblique astigmatism needs no correction.

q.stem: How does the non-contact (air-puff) tonometer detect the moment of corneal flattening?
options: A photodetector receives the most reflected light from an obliquely incident beam when the cornea acts as a plane mirror
A strain gauge in the nozzle detects contact with the cornea
Fluorescein semicircles are aligned by the operator
Ultrasound echoes from the posterior cornea become perpendicular
q.explanation: A parallel beam hits the central cornea at 30 degrees and a detector at 30 degrees on the other side picks up the reflection. This peaks when the cornea is flat. The instrument converts the air force needed to reach this point into IOP, and it must be used at a set distance.

q.stem: An optical pachymeter measures anterior chamber depth using which Purkinje-Sanson images?
options: Images II and III (posterior cornea and anterior lens)
q.explanation: Images I and II (anterior and posterior cornea) give corneal thickness. Images II and III (posterior cornea and anterior lens surface) give anterior chamber depth.

q.stem: In the Jaeger pachymeter, how is corneal thickness read?
options: By tilting the upper of two glass plates until the anterior corneal surface in one half-image meets the posterior surface in the other
By splitting the illuminating beam with a perspex plate and superimposing images
By counting the number of mire steps
q.explanation: The observation axis is set 40 degrees from the perpendicular illumination. The observer's view is split by two plates and the upper one is tilted; the tilt needed to align the front and back surfaces is proportional to thickness. The perspex beam-splitting method belongs to the older Maurice-Giardini pachymeter.

q.stem: Why does an ultrasound pachymeter give a reading only when the probe is perpendicular to the posterior cornea?
options: Because ultrasound cannot pass through tears at an angle
To ensure the true (shortest) thickness is measured, which matters for planning incision depth
To avoid stimulating the blink reflex
q.explanation: Ultrasound pachymetry is more precise than optical methods. Reading only when perpendicular avoids oblique, overestimated values. This precision matters when planning incision depth in graft and refractive surgery.

q.stem: Optical coherence tomography forms cross-sectional retinal images by
options: interference between a reference beam and infrared light reflected from the retina
timing ultrasound echoes from retinal layers
measuring changes in polarisation of light through the nerve fibre layer
detecting the Doppler shift of light from moving red cells
q.explanation: OCT splits infrared light (about 843 nm in the source) into a reference arm reflected from a mirror and a sample arm reflected from the retina. The time-delay differences produce an interference signal, giving resolution down to about 10 µm. Polarisation change is the basis of scanning laser polarimetry, and Doppler shift is the basis of laser Doppler flowmetry.

q.stem: What is the principle of the Scheiner double-pinhole method in automated refraction?
options: An ametropic eye sees one spot; the target is moved until two appear
An ametropic eye sees two spots; moving the target until the spots fuse finds the far point
It judges the position of least blur
It uses polarised light to measure the principal meridians
q.explanation: Two small bundles of light from the Scheiner disc meet at one point on the retina only if the eye is focused for the target. Otherwise two spots are seen. Judging when two spots become one gives a sharper end-point than judging least blur.

q.stem: In an optometer, a +10 D lens sits with its second focal point in the spectacle plane. The target is placed 1 cm closer to the lens than its first focal point. What vergence reaches the spectacle plane?
q.explanation: u = -9 cm gives 1/v = 10 - 11.11 = -1.11, so v = -90 cm. The spectacle plane is 10 cm behind the lens, which puts it 100 cm from the virtual image, so the vergence is -1.00 D. Equivalently, vergence = x F^2 = 0.01 x 100 = 1 D, divergent because the target is inside the focus. The vergence is linear with target displacement, which is the basis of the instrument's calibration.

q.stem: Using the same +10 D optometer lens (second focal point in the spectacle plane), the target is now 2 cm beyond the first focal point. What vergence reaches the spectacle plane?
q.explanation: u = -12 cm gives 1/v = 10 - 8.33 = 1.67, so v = +60 cm. The spectacle plane is 10 cm from the lens, so light converges to a point 50 cm away: +2.00 D. Using x F^2 = 0.02 x 100 = 2 D confirms this; a target outside the focus simulates a convex trial lens. +0.20 D forgets to square F.

q.stem: According to the meridional refractometry principle, what is the minimum number of meridians in which spherical refraction must be measured to find the astigmatic axes and powers?
q.explanation: Measuring the spherical refraction in at least three arbitrary meridians lets the principal axes and their powers be calculated. More meridians improve accuracy at the cost of more complex mathematics. Two arbitrary meridians are not enough unless they happen to be the principal ones.

q.stem: How does a refraction measured with an infrared autorefractor compare with the refraction for visible light, before the instrument corrects for it?
options: It reads about 0.75 to 1.50 D more myopic
It reads about 0.75 to 1.50 D more hypermetropic
It reads about 5 D more hypermetropic
q.explanation: Because of the eye's chromatic aberration, longer infrared wavelengths focus further back, so the eye appears more hypermetropic to infrared by roughly 0.75-1.50 D. Infrared is used because it is invisible and does not stimulate accommodation to the instrument.

q.stem: In which patient is an automatic infrared refractor least likely to give a reliable result?
options: One with a small, distorted pupil after a broad iridectomy
A young emmetrope with clear media
A 6 D myope with clear media and a normal pupil
A patient with 1 D of regular astigmatism
q.explanation: These instruments perform poorly with small or distorted pupils and with media haze bad enough to reduce vision to about 6/18. Regular astigmatism and moderate ametropia are well within their range.

q.stem: In photoscreening of preverbal children, what does the camera capture to detect amblyogenic factors?
options: Alterations of the red reflex photographed with an offset flash
q.explanation: A camera with its flash offset from the lens photographs the red reflex in the horizontal and vertical meridians from a set distance. Refractive error, anisometropia, strabismus and media opacity change the reflex. Trained staff then pick out children for cycloplegic refraction.

q.stem: What is meant by a population inversion in a laser medium?
options: More atoms are in the ground state than excited
More atoms are in the excited (upper) state than in the ground state
All photons travel in opposite directions
The laser cavity mirrors are reversed
q.explanation: Pumping raises electrons to an upper energy level. When excited atoms outnumber unexcited ones, there is a population inversion, which is needed for stimulated emission to dominate. It is called an inversion because it is the opposite of the normal state.

q.stem: How does stimulated emission differ from spontaneous emission?
options: A photon of the right wavelength triggers emission that is coherent with it
It is incoherent and travels in all directions
It happens without any incoming photon
It always emits a longer wavelength than the stimulating photon
q.explanation: Spontaneous emission happens at random and is incoherent and omnidirectional. In stimulated emission, an incoming photon of the transition wavelength triggers the release of an identical photon in phase with it. The resonator amplifies this coherent light.

q.stem: Which statement about the laser resonator is correct?
options: One end mirror is partially transmitting, and the mirror separation is a multiple of the emitted wavelength
The mirrors are placed at random distances
There is only one mirror, at the output end
q.explanation: The light bounces between two mirrors and is amplified while staying in phase. The cavity length must be a whole multiple of the wavelength for resonance. One mirror lets part of the light out as the beam.

q.stem: Which three properties characterise laser light?
q.explanation: Laser light is in phase (coherent), of one wavelength (monochromatic) and made of parallel rays (collimated). Lasers may be CW or pulsed and have many wavelengths, so 'ultraviolet and pulsed' is not a defining property.

q.stem: How are lasers named?
q.explanation: Lasers take their names from the active medium that undergoes stimulated emission, for example argon or krypton (gas), dye (liquid) and Nd:YAG (solid). The pump might be an electrical discharge, another laser or incoherent light.

q.stem: A laser emits only a few lumens yet is exceedingly bright. Why?
options: Its small flux is concentrated in a narrow parallel beam instead of spreading in all directions
Lasers are very efficient energy converters
Its wavelength is always in the ultraviolet
It emits far more total flux than an incandescent bulb
q.explanation: Lasers are in fact very inefficient, and their total output is small. Because the beam does not spread, its luminous intensity is enormous: about 5 lumens can give hundreds of millions of candela, and a 1 W laser gives far higher retinal irradiance than a 100 W bulb.

q.stem: What is the fundamental transverse mode of a laser beam?
options: The point of maximum divergence used for diffuse photocoagulation
The longest wavelength present in the beam
The point of least divergence, where energy can be focused to the smallest spot with a Gaussian profile
q.explanation: At the fundamental mode, energy is most concentrated centrally with a Gaussian fall-off, which gives the smallest focus. This matters most for photodisruption such as YAG capsulotomy, much less for diffuse photocoagulation.

q.stem: A Q-switched Nd:YAG laser delivers a 4 mJ pulse lasting 4 ns. What is the peak power?
q.explanation: Power = energy/time = 0.004 J / 4x10^-9 s = 1x10^6 W. 16 mJ comes from multiplying, and it is an energy unit, not a power. 1 kW and 1 W come from errors with the milli and nano prefixes.

q.stem: An argon photocoagulator is set to 300 mW with a 0.2 s exposure. How much energy is delivered per burn?
q.explanation: Energy = power x time = 0.3 W x 0.2 s = 0.06 J = 60 mJ. 1.5 J (1500 mJ) comes from dividing power by time. 6 mJ is a decimal-place slip.

q.stem: Why is the output of an argon laser usually given in watts but that of a Q-switched Nd:YAG laser in joules?
options: Argon emits more energy than YAG
Argon is a continuous-wave laser with constant power; the YAG gives brief pulses with a power peak, so energy per pulse is the useful measure
YAG lasers do not produce power
Watts are used only for ultraviolet lasers
q.explanation: Continuous-wave lasers deliver steady power, measured in watts. Pulsed lasers produce brief peaks, so the energy per pulse in joules is more convenient. The same energy delivered in a shorter time gives higher power.

q.stem: In Q-switching, what does the shutter in front of one cavity mirror achieve?
options: It produces a continuous beam of constant power
It lets energy build up in the medium, then releases a single pulse lasting about 2-30 ns when opened
It synchronises sub-wavelengths to give picosecond pulses
It doubles the frequency of the light
q.explanation: While the shutter is closed, oscillation is blocked and only spontaneous emission drains the stored energy. Opening it releases one large surge of stimulated emission lasting nanoseconds. Mode locking, a refinement of Q-switching, gives picosecond pulses.

q.stem: Compared with Q-switching, what does mode locking achieve?
options: Pulses of about 30 ms with lower power
Pulses of about 30 ps with up to 100 times the power for the same energy
Continuous output of a single pure wavelength
Pulses of about 30 ns with the same power
q.explanation: Mode locking brings the laser's various sub-wavelengths into phase so that they periodically add up. The result is pulses of about 30 picoseconds and up to 100 times the power of a Q-switched pulse of equal energy.

q.section: Effects of Laser Energy on Tissue
q.stem: Which wavelength range can enter the eye and reach the retina?
q.explanation: Wavelengths from about 400 to 1400 nm are transmitted to the retina. Ultraviolet (such as 193 nm) and far infrared (such as 2940 nm and 10600 nm) are absorbed at the front of the eye.

q.section: Effects of Laser Energy on Tissue
q.stem: A laser pulse of a nanosecond or less strips electrons from molecules to form a plasma whose expansion creates a shock wave. Which lasers act this way?
q.explanation: Very short pulses ionise tissue, and the plasma's mechanical shock wave disrupts it. The source lists Nd:YAG and excimer under ionisation. Argon and CO2 lasers act thermally, and He-Ne is a low-power aiming beam.

q.section: Effects of Laser Energy on Tissue
q.stem: What temperature rise produces photocoagulation, as opposed to vaporisation?
options: Any rise above 1 degree C vaporises tissue
Temperature rise is irrelevant to thermal effects
A rise of about 10-20 degrees C coagulates; reaching 100 degrees C vaporises water and disrupts tissue
q.explanation: Thermal effects happen when the wavelength matches a tissue pigment's absorption and the exposure lasts from microseconds to seconds. Around a 10-20 degree C rise gives coagulation, while 100 degrees C boils water and disrupts tissue.

q.section: Effects of Laser Energy on Tissue
q.stem: Why is argon green preferred to argon blue for photocoagulation near the macula?
options: Melanin absorbs blue but not green
Macular xanthophyll strongly absorbs blue but not green light
q.explanation: Xanthophyll in the inner macular layers absorbs blue light, so blue would damage the inner retina and nerve fibres. Green passes through to be absorbed by melanin in the RPE and choroid and by haemoglobin. Blue at the macula is therefore contraindicated.

q.section: Effects of Laser Energy on Tissue
q.stem: Which type of tissue effect follows exposures of 10 seconds or longer, and which wavelengths are most harmful?
options: Photochemical effects (free radicals); shorter wavelengths such as blue and UV
q.explanation: Long exposures produce reactive free radicals that are toxic to cells, and short wavelengths do this at lower irradiance. This is why argon photocoagulators include a filter to protect the operator from reflected light.

q.stem: Into which safety classes do ophthalmic surgical lasers fall?
q.explanation: Surgical lasers are Class 3b (5-500 mW, can cause significant damage) or Class 4 (above 500 mW, irreversible damage). The eye's focusing can raise retinal irradiance by up to 10^5 times. Classes 1, 2 and 3a are regarded as safe for brief viewing.

q.stem: Which measure protects the surgeon from reflected treatment beam light at the slit-lamp laser?
options: Built-in filters or shutters that operate when the laser fires
q.explanation: Filters absorb the treatment wavelength but let through enough other light for the surgeon to watch the effect. Anyone else who must be in the room wears protective goggles.

q.stem: What does the argon blue-green laser emit?
q.explanation: The classic argon laser emits mostly blue (488 nm) with some green (514 nm). Newer air-cooled units are limited to green. 532 nm is the frequency-doubled Nd:YAG, and 810 nm is the diode.

q.stem: What is the role of the helium-neon laser in ophthalmic laser systems?
options: A low-power red (632.8 nm) aiming beam for lasers with invisible output
q.explanation: The He-Ne laser is a low-power gas laser. Its visible red 632.8 nm beam is used for aiming invisible lasers such as the diode and Nd:YAG.

q.stem: Why can the 810 nm diode laser be used for transscleral cyclophotocoagulation in end-stage glaucoma?
options: Its wavelength penetrates the sclera and is absorbed by melanin
It is absorbed strongly by water at the scleral surface
It is absorbed by xanthophyll in the ciliary body
q.explanation: Diode light scatters little, passes through the sclera and is absorbed only by melanin. It can therefore treat the pigmented ciliary body, or the retina when the view through the pupil is poor, with a probe on the eye's surface.

q.stem: Which dye enhances diode photocoagulation of choroidal neovascular membranes because its absorption peak matches the diode wavelength?
q.explanation: Intravenous indocyanine green absorbs maximally at 800-810 nm, the diode laser's wavelength, so it boosts uptake in vascular targets such as membranes and tumours.

q.stem: Which laser delivers 2940 nm radiation absorbed by water, penetrating less than 1 µm with thermal spread of only 5-15 µm?
q.explanation: Er:YAG at 2940 nm is absorbed very superficially, causing explosive evaporation of tissue with minimal surrounding heat. It has been tried for lens emulsification. CO2 (10600 nm) is also absorbed by water but spreads heat over about 200 µm.

q.stem: Which statement about the Nd:YAG laser used for posterior capsulotomy is correct?
options: It emits invisible 1064 nm infrared, so a red He-Ne aiming beam must be focused at the same point
It emits visible green light at 1064 nm
It uses an ultraviolet aiming beam
q.explanation: Nd:YAG emits 1064 nm infrared and is Q-switched to disrupt the capsule or iris by ionisation. Because the beam is invisible, the He-Ne aiming beam and the treatment beam must focus at the same point before use.

q.stem: What wavelength does a frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser emit, and which laser does its effect resemble?
options: 532 nm, similar to argon green photocoagulation
q.explanation: Doubling the frequency halves the wavelength: 1064/2 = 532 nm, which is green. Its photocoagulation effect is like that of continuous-wave argon green. 2128 nm comes from doubling the wavelength rather than the frequency.

q.stem: The excimer laser emits 193 nm. Using photon energy E (eV) = 1240/wavelength (nm), what is its photon energy, and why does that matter?
options: About 6.4 eV, enough to break intramolecular bonds
About 1.2 eV, enough to coagulate tissue
About 0.16 eV, too low to affect bonds
About 64 eV, causing ionising radiation damage deep in the eye
q.explanation: 1240/193 = 6.4 eV per photon, which can break molecular bonds directly and ablate a precise depth of corneal tissue with little heat spread. 1.2 eV is the value for the 1064 nm Nd:YAG. 0.16 eV comes from inverting the ratio.

q.stem: Which statement about the excimer laser is correct?
options: It emits infrared light that penetrates deeply into the stroma
It requires a He-Ne aiming beam because it is a solid-state laser
It uses an argon-fluoride excited dimer and causes little heating of adjacent tissue
q.explanation: 'Excimer' comes from 'excited dimer' (ArF). Its 193 nm UV is highly absorbed by the cornea, so penetration is shallow and ablation depth precise. Although the treated volume gets very hot, little heat is produced overall, which makes it suitable for PRK, LASIK and PTK.

q.stem: What is true of the CO2 laser?
options: It emits 193 nm and ablates by breaking bonds
It emits 10600 nm, strongly absorbed by water, with about 90% of energy absorbed within 200 µm; its effects are purely thermal
It is widely used for retinal photocoagulation
It penetrates the sclera to treat the ciliary body
q.explanation: CO2 mid-infrared light is absorbed by water at the tissue surface, giving a nearly bloodless incision in general surgery. The source notes it has yet to find a role in ophthalmology.

q.stem: Which laser emits 1053 nm in picosecond pulses at very high repetition rates and has been used experimentally to dissect tissue and for intrastromal corneal ablation?
q.explanation: The neodymium-yttrium-lithium-fluoride laser gives picosecond 1053 nm pulses that can dissect rather than disrupt tissue. The holmium laser has been used for sclerostomy and thermokeratoplasty.

q.stem: Which laser has been used for thermokeratoplasty to change corneal curvature and for sclerostomy in glaucoma?
q.explanation: The holmium laser has been used for both of these.

q.section: Investigational Applications of Lasers in Ophthalmology
q.stem: What gives a confocal optical system its increased contrast and resolution?
options: A very wide field of illumination
Illumination and imaging focus on the same small point, with a pinhole or slit rejecting scattered light
Doubling of the image with a Wollaston prism
q.explanation: Confocal systems light up and view a tiny spot, often with a laser source, and view through a pinhole or slit. This removes scattered light from other depths. The same principle underlies confocal microscopy of the cornea and the CSLO.

q.section: Investigational Applications of Lasers in Ophthalmology
q.stem: Scanning laser polarimetry estimates retinal nerve fibre layer thickness because the RNFL
options: is birefringent; the retardation of polarised light correlates with its thickness
q.explanation: The parallel axons of the RNFL change the polarisation of light passing through them. The amount of change (retardation) tracks RNFL thickness and is used to detect glaucomatous damage.

q.section: Investigational Applications of Lasers in Ophthalmology
q.stem: Which technique uses a 670 nm diode confocal scanning laser ophthalmoscope to make a three-dimensional topographic map of the optic nerve head?
q.explanation: Confocal scanning laser tomography builds a 3D map of the disc for assessing glaucoma. Polarimetry measures RNFL retardation, and Doppler flowmetry measures blood flow.

q.section: Investigational Applications of Lasers in Ophthalmology
q.stem: In laser interferometry to estimate potential acuity behind a cataract, what happens to the interference grating when the two laser sources are moved closer together?
q.explanation: The fringes form where the two beams overlap on the retina, despite cataract or refractive error. Bringing the sources closer together widens the fringe spacing, so the grating gets coarser. The finest grating the patient can still resolve estimates macular potential.

q.section: Investigational Applications of Lasers in Ophthalmology
q.stem: Laser Doppler flowmetry measures retinal capillary blood flow by detecting
options: changes in polarisation in the nerve fibre layer
the frequency shift of light reflected from moving blood cells
the time delay of reflected infrared light
q.explanation: Light reflected from moving red cells comes back at a slightly different frequency, and a bigger shift means faster flow. The time delay of reflected infrared light is the basis of OCT.

q.section: Investigational Applications of Lasers in Ophthalmology
q.stem: What is laser microperimetry used for?
options: Measuring the light sensitivity of very small retinal areas to find small scotomas
q.explanation: Laser microperimetry tests the light sensitivity of tiny retinal loci, which lets small scotomas be mapped precisely. The CSLO can also be used for microperimetry.

q.stem: A long-standing myope complains that a new pair of spectacles of identical power feels wrong; the dispenser changed the lens form. Which lens form do many such myopes prefer to keep?
options: Biconcave lenses with equal surface curves
Deep meniscus lenses with a steep front curve
Lenticular lenses with a carrier rim
q.explanation: Myopes are notoriously intolerant of a change in lens form, and many like to continue with plano-concave 'flats' even when another form would be optically better. A biconcave or steep meniscus form may be optically fine but feels different. Lenticular forms are for very high powers and are not what such patients are used to.

q.stem: When measuring uniocular acuity in a patient with nystagmus, how should the fellow eye be managed?
options: Leave it uncovered and test binocular acuity only
Place a pinhole in front of it
Occlude it completely with an opaque occluder
Fog it with a high plus lens rather than occlude it
q.explanation: Completely covering one eye increases the nystagmus and lowers the measured acuity of the eye being tested. Blurring the fellow eye with a strong plus lens removes its useful vision while keeping enough light and fusion input to damp the nystagmus. A pinhole or no cover would not prevent the fellow eye from seeing the chart.

q.stem: Why is detailed examination of the fundi usually left until after the refraction has been completed?
options: The pupils must be dilated before any fundus view is possible
Bright ophthalmoscope light causes photostress that temporarily lowers acuity
Ophthalmoscopy induces accommodation that lasts several hours
The retinoscope beam damages the macula if used after ophthalmoscopy
q.explanation: Prolonged bright illumination of the macula produces photostress, transiently reducing visual acuity and spoiling the subjective refraction. A brief look is acceptable early on if acuity is very poor, to exclude pathology. Ophthalmoscopy does not induce lasting accommodation, and dilation is not mandatory for a view.

q.stem: A patient has a manifest squint on cover testing but no diplopia. Which part of the routine examination is likely to be impossible?
options: Testing muscle balance with the Maddox rod and Maddox wing
q.explanation: A manifest squint without diplopia implies absent binocular single vision. The Maddox rod and wing are dissociation tests of heterophoria that require the two eyes to function together, so they cannot be performed meaningfully. Retinoscopy, cross-cylinder testing and uniocular acuity are all monocular procedures.

q.stem: Where should a high power trial lens be placed in the trial frame?
options: In the front cell, furthest from the eye
In any cell, as power is unaffected by position
In the middle cell, alongside the cylinder
In the back cell, nearest the eye
q.explanation: High power lenses go in the back cell so that they sit as close to the eye as possible and at a known back vertex distance. A lens of high power changes its effective power noticeably when moved along the visual axis, so placing it in a front cell would alter the result.

q.stem: During retinoscopy the examiner uses the right eye to examine the patient's right eye. What is the main reason?
options: To avoid blocking the patient's view of the distant target and so prevent accommodation
Because the examiner's dominant eye gives a brighter reflex
To keep the examiner's working distance exactly 1 m
To align the retinoscope with the patient's angle kappa
q.explanation: Using matching eyes lets the examiner work close to the patient's visual axis without obstructing the distance fixation target. If the patient looks at the examiner instead, accommodation is stimulated, betrayed by pupil constriction and a harder-to-see reflex. Working distance is usually 2/3 m and is unrelated to which eye is used.

q.stem: In which of the following patients is cycloplegic retinoscopy particularly indicated?
options: A patient with keratoconus and a swirling reflex
A young child with a latent or manifest squint
An adult with stable myopia wearing contact lenses
q.explanation: Young children, and children with latent or manifest squint, have active accommodation that can mask hypermetropia, so the ciliary muscle is paralysed to reveal the true refractive error. A 60-year-old has little accommodation left, and cycloplegia does not help with keratoconic reflexes.

q.stem: A refractionist performs retinoscopy at a working distance of 50 cm and wishes to place a 'working distance lens' in the trial frame first. Which lens is required?
q.explanation: The working distance lens has a power equal to the dioptric value of the working distance: 1/0.50 m = +2.00 D. +1.50 DS is the lens for 2/3 m, +0.50 DS confuses metres with dioptres, and a minus lens is the sign error (minus is what you add afterwards if no working lens was used).

q.stem: Retinoscopy at 2/3 m without a working distance lens shows neutralisation in all meridians with +3.00 DS. What is the refractive correction?
q.explanation: At 2/3 m the examiner's position contributes 1/0.667 = 1.50 D, so 1.50 D must be subtracted from the gross finding: +3.00 - 1.50 = +1.50 DS. Adding instead of subtracting gives +4.50 DS, and ignoring the working distance gives +3.00 DS.

q.stem: Retinoscopy is performed at 50 cm with no working distance lens. An 'against' movement is neutralised with -1.50 DS in every meridian. What is the patient's spherical correction?
q.explanation: The working distance correction at 50 cm is 1/0.5 = 2.00 D, which is always subtracted (added as minus): -1.50 + (-2.00) = -3.50 DS. +0.50 DS results from adding +2.00 instead, -1.50 DS ignores the working distance, and -2.00 DS is just the working distance itself.

q.stem: Viewing through the working distance lens, the retinoscopy reflex moves 'with' the streak. What should be added, and what is the end point if neutral falls between lens steps?
options: Add concave lenses; take the brightest reflex as the end point
Add convex lenses; take the dimmest reflex as the end point
Add convex lenses; take reversal of the reflex as the end point
Add concave lenses; take reversal of the reflex as the end point
q.explanation: A 'with' movement means the far point lies behind the examiner, so plus power is added; concave lenses are added for 'against'. When neutral lies between available lens powers, the first lens that reverses the movement is accepted as the end point.

q.stem: Near the point of reversal, a correcting cylinder lies 5 degrees off the true axis of astigmatism. Approximately how far is the retinoscopy reflex misaligned from the streak?
q.explanation: Close to reversal the reflex is misaligned by roughly six times the cylinder error: 6 x 5 = 30 degrees. This magnification is why the cylinder needs only a small rotation before rechecking, and why the method locates the axis very precisely. A 1:1 relationship (5 degrees) underestimates the effect.

q.stem: During cycloplegic retinoscopy of a small child using hand-held spheres only, how can the axes of astigmatism be identified?
options: The reflex moves 'against' only in the steepest meridian
Spheres alone cannot reveal astigmatic axes
The reflex becomes brightest when the streak is at 45 degrees to a principal meridian
The pupillary reflex aligns with the streak only when the streak lies in a principal meridian
q.explanation: When the streak is rotated, the reflex stays parallel to it only in the two principal meridians; in between it moves obliquely. This allows the axes to be found without cylinders, which is useful when holding loose lenses before a child. Brightness at 45 degrees and the direction of movement do not locate the axes.

q.stem: After correcting for working distance, the trial frame contains +4.00 DS / -1.50 DC. Subjectively the patient accepts only -1.00 DC. What should the sphere become?
q.explanation: The principal meridians of the retinoscopy result are +4.00 and +2.50. With +4.00/-1.00 the weaker meridian receives +3.00, overcorrecting it by +0.50, so the sphere must drop to +3.50 (giving meridians +3.50 and +2.50). Keeping +4.00 leaves the overcorrection; +4.50 makes it worse; +3.00 undercorrects both meridians.

q.stem: Retinoscopy yields meridians of +2.50 and +4.00 D (after working distance), corrected as +2.50 DS / +1.50 DC. The patient accepts only +1.00 DC. What is the effect?
options: The weaker meridian is overcorrected by 0.50 D and the sphere must be reduced
Both meridians become overcorrected by 0.50 D
The stronger meridian is overcorrected by 0.50 D and the sphere must be increased
The stronger meridian is undercorrected by 0.50 D and the sphere need not change
q.explanation: +2.50/+1.00 gives meridians of +2.50 and +3.50, leaving the +4.00 meridian undercorrected by 0.50 D. Undercorrection of a hypermetropic meridian is well tolerated, so no change to the sphere is needed. This is the advantage of plus cylinders with plus spheres; the minus cylinder route overcorrects the weaker meridian instead.

q.stem: Gross retinoscopy at 2/3 m (no working lens) neutralises at +3.50 along 90 and +5.00 along 180. A refractionist who pairs plus cylinders with plus spheres would record which correction?
q.explanation: Subtract 1.50 D: the 90 meridian needs +2.00 and the 180 meridian +3.50. The sphere covers the lower meridian (+2.00) and a +1.50 cylinder adds power in the 180 meridian, so its axis lies at 90. Forgetting the working distance gives +3.50/+1.50; putting the axis at 180 adds the power to the wrong meridian; +3.50/-1.50 x 90 swaps the meridian powers.

q.stem: Before any lenses, the retinoscopy reflex moves 'with' in one meridian and 'against' in the other. Which lens combination is advised?
options: Spheres alone, averaging the two end points
Minus spheres to neutralise one meridian, then plus cylinders for the other
Minus spheres and minus cylinders together
Plus spheres to neutralise one meridian, then minus cylinders for the other
q.explanation: With mixed movements, one meridian is neutralised with a sphere and the other with a stronger cylinder of opposite sign. Using minus spheres with plus cylinders is preferred because the 'with' movement produced while adding plus cylinders makes the axis easier to locate than an 'against' movement.

q.stem: Retinoscopy at 2/3 m (no working lens) is recorded on a cross: the horizontal meridian neutralises at +3.00 and the vertical meridian at +4.50. What is the prescription in minus cylinder form?
q.explanation: After subtracting 1.50 D, the horizontal meridian needs +1.50 and the vertical +3.00. A +3.00 sphere suits the vertical meridian and a -1.50 cylinder must act in the horizontal meridian, so its axis is at 90 (a cylinder's axis lies 90 degrees from the meridian it powers). Axis 180 puts the cylinder in the wrong meridian, and +4.50 forgets the working distance.

q.stem: Retinoscopy at 2/3 m (no working lens) neutralises the vertical meridian with -1.00 and the horizontal meridian with -2.50. What is the correction?
q.explanation: Adding -1.50 D for working distance gives -2.50 in the vertical meridian and -4.00 in the horizontal. Minus cylinder form: -2.50 sphere plus a -1.50 cylinder acting horizontally, i.e. axis 90 (equivalently -4.00/+1.50 x 180). -1.00/-1.50 omits the working distance, and the other two place the cylinder in the wrong meridian.

q.stem: With the trial frame empty, no retinoscopy reflex can be identified in a patient with clear media; the pupil looks dim and diffuse. What is the suggested next step?
options: Repeat retinoscopy through a strong convex and then a strong concave lens, e.g. +/-7.00 DS
Abandon objective refraction and proceed directly to subjective testing
Dilate the pupil and repeat with the same lenses
Switch to a 1 m working distance to brighten the reflex
q.explanation: A very dim, diffuse reflex suggests a high refractive error. Placing a strong plus and then a strong minus lens (around 7 D) will bring the reflex into view with one of them, and the direct ophthalmoscope can also distinguish high myopia from high hypermetropia. Changing working distance or dilating does not overcome the large error.

q.stem: An elderly patient with nuclear sclerosis has a bright central pupillary reflex on retinoscopy. How should the end point be judged?
options: Neutralise the darkest part of the reflex
Average the central and peripheral end points
Concentrate on the central zone, which contains the visual axis
Neutralise the peripheral zone, which is relatively myopic
q.explanation: In nucleosclerosis the central zone is relatively myopic compared with the periphery, making the centre appear bright. Because the visual axis passes through the centre, the end point should be judged there even if it is less crisp. The periphery is relatively hypermetropic, not myopic.

q.stem: During retinoscopy of a dilated pupil, two reflexes move towards and away from each other like scissor blades. What causes this and how do the authors suggest the end point is taken?
options: Oblique astigmatism; rotate the streak until the reflexes are parallel
Different refraction in different pupil zones; take the end point when the brighter reflex reverses
Accommodative fluctuation; take the end point when the dimmer reflex reverses
Corneal scarring; take the end point when both reflexes disappear
q.explanation: Scissor shadows arise because one part of the pupil is relatively myopic and another relatively hypermetropic to the plane of observation; they are commoner with dilated pupils and near the end point. The traditional end point is when the two reflexes meet centrally, but the authors find it easier to use reversal of the brighter blade.

q.stem: Which retinoscopic appearance is characteristic of keratoconus?
options: A red reflex that is absent centrally but normal peripherally only after dilation
A swirling reflex with a dark reflex at the cone apex (oil-drop sign)
A sharply defined 'with' movement at all powers
A bright central reflex with a dark periphery
q.explanation: Keratoconus produces a swirling reflex, and the apex of the cone appears darker than the surrounding cornea, the oil-drop sign. An end point may be impossible to find, so subjective testing must be relied upon. A bright centre with darker periphery is the nucleosclerosis pattern.

q.stem: Gross retinoscopy at 2/3 m without a working distance lens gives +2.00 DS / -2.00 DC x 180. Following the usual advice before starting the subjective refraction, which lenses should be in the frame?
q.explanation: First correct for working distance: +2.00 - 1.50 = +0.50 DS. Because patients seldom accept the full cylinder, it is then reduced by about a quarter: 2.00 x 0.75 = 1.50 DC. +2.00 forgets the working distance, -2.00 DC skips the cylinder reduction, and +3.50 adds the working distance instead of subtracting it.

q.stem: When verifying the sphere, what size of step is appropriate for a patient with poor visual acuity?
options: 0.12 DS, to compensate for the poor acuity
0.50 DS, because small 0.25 DS changes may not be appreciated
q.explanation: Patients with good acuity can discriminate a 0.25 DS change, but those with poor acuity may only notice larger steps such as 0.50 DS. Smaller steps would not be detected; 1.00 D steps would be too coarse for most.

q.stem: In the subjective refraction, after the sphere has been verified, what is the correct order of cylinder refinement?
options: Check the cylinder power first, then its axis
Check the cylinder axis first, then its power
Measure near acuity first, then the cylinder
Recheck the duochrome first, then the axis
q.explanation: The axis is refined with the cross-cylinder before the power, because an axis error distorts the power reading. If the cylinder power changes considerably, the sphere should be rechecked afterwards.

q.stem: A myope's monocular duochrome shows the red letters only slightly clearer. Binocularly the green letters appear clearer. What adjustment is advised?
options: Leave the prescription unchanged since monocular results are correct
Reduce the minus power by about 0.25 DS in one or both eyes
Add a further -0.25 DS to both eyes
Add base-in prism to relax convergence
q.explanation: Green clearer binocularly means the patient is relatively over-minused when the eyes work together and would need to accommodate. Adding about +0.25 DS (i.e. reducing the minus) makes red clearer binocularly so that the patient is comfortable and not accommodating. Adding more minus would worsen the problem.

q.stem: After subjective refraction a -10.00 DS lens sits in the back cell of the trial frame at a back vertex distance of 12 mm. What is the equivalent power at the corneal plane (to the nearest 0.25 D)?
q.explanation: Effective power at the cornea = F / (1 - dF) = -10 / (1 - 0.012 x -10) = -10 / 1.12 = -8.93, so about -9.00 D. A minus lens moved closer to the eye must be weaker; -11.25 D comes from the sign error (dividing by 0.88). This is why the BVD is recorded whenever the sphere exceeds 5 D.

q.stem: A +10.00 DS correction was found with a back vertex distance of 12 mm, but the chosen frame will hold the lens 15 mm from the cornea. What power should be ordered (nearest 0.25 D)?
q.explanation: The lens focuses 100 mm behind itself, i.e. 88 mm behind the cornea; that is the eye's far point. From 15 mm the required focal length is 88 + 15 = 103 mm, so F = 1000/103 = +9.71, about +9.75 D. A plus lens moved away from the eye becomes effectively stronger, so a weaker lens is needed; +10.25 D is the wrong direction.

q.stem: With a Maddox rod in place, a patient sees the spot when the right eye alone is open and the line when the left eye alone is open, but never both together with both eyes open. What does this indicate?
options: Binocular vision is defective or absent
A large vertical phoria that needs full prism correction
The Maddox rod is in the wrong orientation
q.explanation: If each target is seen uniocularly but not simultaneously with both eyes uncovered, one eye is being suppressed, indicating defective or absent binocular vision. Orientation of the rod would change the line's direction, not whether it is seen. Significant phorias are often treated with less than the full measured prism.

q.stem: What is the most frequent reason patients return for a re-test after refraction, according to the text?
options: A reading addition that is too strong
Failure to record the back vertex distance
q.explanation: Prescribing too strong a near addition is the commonest cause of return visits, as the reading distance becomes uncomfortably close. Normally no more than +2.50 DS is given, although pseudophakic patients often prefer +3.00 DS.

q.stem: A pseudophakic patient with no accommodation is given their distance correction plus a +3.00 DS reading addition. At what distance will print be in sharp focus?
q.explanation: With no accommodation, the near add alone sets the focus: 1/3.00 = 0.333 m = 33 cm. A +2.50 add would focus at 40 cm and +4.00 at 25 cm; 3 cm confuses dioptres with centimetres. Pseudophakes often prefer +3.00 DS, whereas phakic presbyopes normally need no more than +2.50 DS.

q.stem: Maddox wing testing shows orthophoria for distance but a large exophoria for near in a symptomatic patient. What is the recommended management?
options: Base-in prisms in the reading spectacles
Base-out prisms in the distance spectacles
q.explanation: Distance orthophoria with a large near exophoria indicates convergence insufficiency, and symptomatic cases are treated by strengthening convergence with exercises. Base-in prisms relieve symptoms temporarily but allow convergence to weaken further, so stronger and stronger prisms become necessary.

q.stem: Aphakic spectacles of +12.00 D are made with each optical centre 2 mm temporal to the pupil. What total horizontal prism results?
q.explanation: Prentice's rule per lens: P = F x d(cm) = 12 x 0.2 = 2.4 prism dioptres, so 4.8 in total. The eyes look through the nasal parts of plus lenses whose bases point towards the optical centres, i.e. temporally, giving base out. Using millimetres instead of centimetres gives 48. Poor centration like this commonly causes intolerance of aphakic glasses.

q.stem: A child's -6.00 D spectacles are in a frame that is too wide, so each optical centre lies 3 mm temporal to the pupil. What is the total induced horizontal prism?
q.explanation: Each lens: 6 x 0.3 = 1.8 prism dioptres, total 3.6. The eye looks through the nasal portion of a minus lens, whose thicker edge (base) lies nasally, so the prism is base in. 1.8 is one lens only, base out is the plus-lens answer, and 18 results from forgetting to convert mm to cm.

q.stem: When measuring interpupillary distance with a millimetre rule, why is the measurement taken from limbus to limbus rather than from pupil to pupil?
options: To avoid error from differences or changes in pupil size
Because pupils are always decentred nasally
To include the angle kappa in the measurement
Because the limbus marks the visual axis
q.explanation: Taking the measurement between corresponding limbal edges (nasal limbus of one eye, temporal limbus of the other) eliminates inaccuracy caused by unequal or changing pupil diameters. The limbus does not mark the visual axis; the distance between visual axes for distance is about 1 mm less than the anatomical measurement.

q.stem: The anatomical interpupillary distance of an adult measures 65 mm. What value best represents the separation of the visual axes for distance vision when centring spectacles?
q.explanation: The distance between the visual axes for distance fixation is roughly 1 mm less than the anatomical interpupillary distance, so about 64 mm. 66 mm adds instead of subtracting, and 61 mm is closer to a near centration distance.

q.stem: Which patient is the exception to the rule that a large cylinder should not be given to someone who has never worn one?
q.explanation: New wearers are usually 'broken in' to cylinders gradually because a full astigmatic correction causes distortion. Pseudophakic patients, however, tolerate the full astigmatic correction well. A myope in particular should not have the cylinder axis changed without compelling reason.

q.stem: Subjective refraction finds that a hypermetrope accepts a maximum of +2.75 DS and a myope's best sphere is -3.25 DS. Following the hints to avoid intolerance, what should be prescribed?
q.explanation: Both are left about 0.25 DS undercorrected. The hypermetrope at +2.50 still sees distant objects clearly, and the myope at -3.00 does not need to accommodate for distance. Overcorrecting either (more plus for the hypermetrope, more minus for the myope) causes blur or accommodative strain.

q.stem: A patient's prescription has changed by -0.25 DS since last year and they are happy with their current spectacles. What is the appropriate advice?
options: Increase the reading addition to compensate
Do not advise new glasses for a change they would not notice
q.explanation: A satisfactory prescription should not be altered without a definite reason, and patients should not be told to buy new spectacles for a minor change they cannot appreciate subjectively. Changing lens type or the add would introduce new problems.

q.section: Notes on the Management of Refractive Errors in Children
q.stem: The guidance on children's refractive errors applies to the age group at risk of squint and amblyopia. What age range is this?
q.explanation: The at-risk period for developing squint or amblyopia is taken as birth to about 8 years. This is the window in which refractive correction can influence visual development.

q.section: Notes on the Management of Refractive Errors in Children
q.stem: In which situation does hypermetropia in a child require full correction?
options: When there is an associated exotropia
When there is an associated esophoria or esotropia
Only after the age of 8 years
q.explanation: Hypermetropia is common in children, but in the presence of esophoria or esotropia it should be fully corrected, removing the accommodative drive to converge. Correction is also wise when there is a family history of esotropia. Myopia, not hypermetropia, is corrected to help control exodeviations.

q.section: Notes on the Management of Refractive Errors in Children
q.stem: Cycloplegic refraction of a 4-year-old gives RE +1.50 DS and LE +3.00 DS. What is the main concern?
options: Refractive amblyopia of the right eye; the anisometropia should be corrected
No concern, as the anisometropia is under 2 D
Refractive amblyopia of the left eye; the anisometropia should be corrected
Myopic shift of the right eye with growth
