q.explanation: The anisometropia is 3.00 - 1.50 = 1.50 D of hypermetropia, more than the 1 D threshold. The more hypermetropic eye (LE) receives the more blurred image because accommodation is driven by the better eye, so it is at risk of amblyopia and the difference must be corrected.

q.section: Notes on the Management of Refractive Errors in Children
q.stem: A hypermetropic child wears glasses for the first time and complains that vision is blurred. What is the likely explanation?
options: Habitual accommodation has not yet relaxed
The child has developed latent myopia
The prescription has been overcorrected by working distance
q.explanation: Uncorrected hypermetropic children compensate by accommodating extra; with new glasses this accommodation may not relax at once, causing blur. It usually relaxes within days if the glasses are worn, so parents should be warned. If not, the prescription may be reduced temporarily or a short course of cycloplegic used.

q.section: Notes on the Management of Refractive Errors in Children
q.stem: Why should myopia be corrected in a child with an exophoria or exotropia?
options: To relax accommodation and reduce convergence
To slow axial growth of the eye
To induce a compensating base-in prism
To stimulate accommodation and the associated convergence
q.explanation: Correcting myopia makes the child accommodate for near, and accommodative convergence helps control the exodeviation. Relaxing accommodation would reduce convergence and worsen it. Glasses do not stop the myopia from progressing as the eye grows.

q.section: Notes on the Management of Refractive Errors in Children
q.stem: Cycloplegic refraction of a 2-year-old shows -12.00 DS in both eyes. Which prescription follows the guidance?
q.explanation: High myopia should be corrected as soon as it is found because it impairs development, but full correction is not tolerated, so the eyes are left 1-2 D undercorrected: -10.50 DS is 1.50 D under. Full correction (-12.00) or overcorrection would be poorly tolerated, and delaying treatment risks developmental delay.

q.section: Notes on the Management of Refractive Errors in Children
q.stem: Why can young children achieve good results with spectacles even in large degrees of anisometropia, when adults could not?
options: Children suppress the more myopic eye permanently
Children's eyes have greater amplitude of accommodation
Children's spectacles have shorter vertex distances
The young brain tolerates much greater aniseikonia
q.explanation: Spectacles started early can succeed in uniocular moderate or high myopia because the developing visual system copes with far larger image size differences than an adult's. If glasses fail, a contact lens on the myopic eye may work, although contact lens wear is practically demanding in children.

q.section: Notes on the Management of Refractive Errors in Children
q.stem: A healthy 18-month-old has 2.00 D of astigmatism with no squint or anisometropia. What is the usual approach?
options: Observe, as astigmatism often decreases by 2.5-3 years
Prescribe half the cylinder as a spherical equivalent
q.explanation: Most babies have considerable astigmatism that often lessens or vanishes by 2.5-3 years, so astigmatism alone rarely needs correction in infants. From 3 years, astigmatism of 1 D or more that reduces acuity should be corrected.

q.section: Notes on the Management of Refractive Errors in Children
q.stem: At an annual review, a cooperative child wearing -2.00 DS is retinoscoped at 2/3 m through the glasses with an added +1.50 D fogging lens. The reflex shows 'against' movement, neutralised by a further -0.75 DS. What is the new correction?
q.explanation: The +1.50 lens cancels the working distance, so any extra lens needed for neutral is the change in prescription: -2.00 + (-0.75) = -2.75 DS. -1.25 adds the change with the wrong sign, -2.00 ignores it, and -4.25 subtracts the working distance a second time although it is already compensated by the fogging lens.

q.section: Notes on the Management of Refractive Errors in Children
q.stem: A child repeatedly refuses to keep on newly acquired glasses. What should parents be advised to look for first?
options: Sore spots or chafing from the frame
Signs of amblyopia in the fellow eye
q.explanation: Physical discomfort is a common and easily missed cause of non-tolerance; parents who do not wear spectacles may not think of it. Checking for sore spots or chafing where the frame rests is the first simple step.

q.stem: A presbyope wants one eye left able to read at 40 cm without spectacles after refractive surgery. What postoperative refraction should be targeted in that eye?
q.explanation: The far point of an unaccommodating myopic eye lies at 1/|error|: for 40 cm the error must be 1/0.40 = 2.50 D of myopia. -1.00 D (a margin-of-safety target) gives a far point of 1 m, and +2.50 is the sign error; a hypermetropic eye cannot focus near without accommodation.

q.stem: Why do some surgeons aim for -1.00 D rather than emmetropia after refractive surgery?
options: It gives the best uncorrected distance acuity
It reduces the risk of corneal ectasia
It leaves a margin of error so the eye is less likely to end up hypermetropic
It prevents regression of the treatment
q.explanation: A small myopic target protects against overshooting into hypermetropia, which patients particularly dislike. It does not give the best distance acuity (emmetropia does) and has no bearing on ectasia or regression.

q.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the ways of altering the refractive state of the eye?
options: Changing the depth of the anterior chamber
Changing the refractive power of an ocular medium
Changing the axial length of the eye
q.explanation: Refraction can be altered by changing the power of any ocular medium, the anterior chamber depth or the axial length. Pupil size affects depth of focus and aberrations but does not change the refractive error itself.

q.stem: Within what range of refractive error is corneal refractive surgery usually limited?
q.explanation: Corneal surgery generally treats from about +4.00 to -10.00 D. Almost any spherical error can be corrected by replacing the crystalline lens with an intraocular lens, which is why lens-based surgery covers the extremes.

q.stem: A spectacle wearer with good acuity is -7.00 D in each eye. Only the right eye will be treated, the left being corrected by spectacles. What is the least myopic target for the right eye that keeps anisometropia within the level most patients tolerate?
q.explanation: Patients are unlikely to tolerate more than 2.50 D of anisometropia unless they wear a contact lens in the unoperated eye. So the right eye must be within 2.50 D of -7.00: -7.00 + 2.50 = -4.50 D. Plano gives 7 D of anisometropia, -2.50 D confuses the threshold with the target, and -9.50 D moves the wrong way.

q.stem: In monovision, one eye is corrected for distance and the other left myopic for near. If the near eye is -2.50 D and the patient has 1.00 D of accommodation left, what is that eye's range of clear vision?
q.explanation: The far point is 1/2.50 = 40 cm. With full accommodation the eye's total near power is 3.50 D, so the near point is 1/3.50 = 28.6 cm. 33 cm would require only 0.50 D of accommodation, and 'infinity to 40 cm' describes an emmetrope with 2.50 D of accommodation. Up to half of patients cannot adapt to monovision.

q.stem: Why is 21 years generally considered the minimum age for corneal refractive surgery?
options: The cornea is too thin before 21 years
Childhood myopia may not stabilise until the third decade
Accommodation is too strong before 21 years
Excimer lasers are licensed only for adults over 21
q.explanation: Refraction and corneal topography must be stable before surgery, and myopia beginning in childhood can continue to progress into the third decade. Corneal thickness and accommodation are not the reasons given.

q.stem: Contact lens wear causes corneal warpage that must settle before refractive surgery. Which type of lens is associated with the longest period of topographic change after discontinuation?
q.explanation: Topography changes for about fifteen weeks after PMMA, ten after gas permeable and five after soft lenses are stopped. Surgery should be delayed until the topography is stable.

q.stem: If each excimer laser pulse removes 0.4 microns of corneal tissue, how many pulses are needed to ablate 60 microns at the centre of the treatment zone?
q.explanation: Number of pulses = 60 / 0.4 = 150. 24 comes from multiplying instead of dividing, and 1500 and 15 are factor-of-ten errors. Each pulse ablates only 0.4-0.5 microns, which is what makes precise sculpting possible.

q.stem: A myopic PRK treatment is applied over a 4 mm diameter zone. What is the main disadvantage compared with a 6-7 mm zone?
options: Deeper ablation is needed for the same correction
Haloes around lights when the pupil dilates
More tissue is removed peripherally than centrally
q.explanation: With a small 3.5-4 mm zone, the edge of the ablation falls within a dilated pupil and causes haloes around lights. A wider zone reduces this but needs a deeper ablation for the same refractive effect, so 'deeper ablation' is the disadvantage of the wide zone, not the small one. Myopic treatment flattens the cornea by removing more tissue centrally.

q.stem: Which of the following is associated with PRK for higher degrees of myopia?
options: More predictable outcome than for low myopia
Greater likelihood of late regression towards myopia
q.explanation: Higher myopic treatments are less predictable, more prone to late myopic regression and carry a greater risk of sub-epithelial scarring that causes glare or reduced best corrected acuity. A hypermetropic drift is characteristic of radial keratotomy, not PRK.

q.stem: Why do scanning slit and flying spot excimer systems need a system to fix or track the eye?
options: They use an infrared rather than ultraviolet beam
Their lower energy output prolongs the treatment time
They ablate deeper per pulse than broad-beam lasers
q.explanation: Scanning and flying-spot delivery have lower energy output than a broad beam, so treatment takes longer and eye movement during that time must be controlled by fixation or tracking. They are not limited to hypermetropia and still use the excimer ultraviolet wavelength.

q.stem: How does an ablatable PMMA mask allow excimer correction of astigmatism or hypermetropia?
options: The mask reflects the beam onto the steep meridian
The mask absorbs all laser energy outside the central 3 mm
Thinner parts of the mask are ablated through first, allowing deeper ablation of the underlying cornea
Thicker parts of the mask focus the beam more strongly
q.explanation: The mask shields the cornea, and the laser must cut through it before reaching the corneal surface. Where the mask is thinner it is breached first, so the cornea underneath receives more ablation. Shaping the mask therefore shapes the ablation profile, e.g. more peripheral ablation to steepen the cornea for hypermetropia.

q.stem: To correct regular astigmatism with the excimer laser, which corneal meridian must have its curvature reduced the most?
options: The meridian at 45 degrees to the steepest
q.explanation: Regular astigmatism is treated by flattening the steepest meridian more than any other. With a widening slit beam, ablation is uniform along the slit's length, so curvature is reduced only in the meridian across which the slit widens. Flattening all meridians equally treats only the spherical component.

q.stem: What ablation profile is needed to correct hypermetropia with the excimer laser?
options: More tissue removed peripherally than centrally, steepening the cornea
Ablation confined to a single meridian
Uniform depth ablation across the whole zone
More tissue removed centrally than peripherally, flattening the cornea
q.explanation: Hypermetropia needs more converging power, so the central cornea must be steepened by ablating more peripheral tissue. Central ablation flattens the cornea and corrects myopia. Hypermetropic treatment is harder and less widely used than myopic treatment.

q.stem: In LASIK, how is the excimer laser treatment delivered?
options: To the stromal bed beneath a hinged lamellar flap that is then replaced
To a donor lenticule shaped on a cryolathe
To the corneal epithelium after it is scraped away
Within a PMMA ring tunnel in the mid-peripheral stroma
q.explanation: A microkeratome cuts a uniform-thickness lamellar flap left attached at a hinge. The flap is lifted, the bared stroma is reshaped by the excimer laser, and the flap is replaced in the same orientation. Epithelial removal is PRK, and the cryolathe belongs to keratomileusis.

q.stem: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of LASIK over PRK?
options: Better predictability in very high myopia
Less sub-epithelial scarring and myopic regression
It is the only laser technique that can correct astigmatism
q.explanation: Compared with PRK, LASIK appears to give less sub-epithelial scarring and regression, faster stabilisation and better predictability for very high myopia, and the flap can be re-lifted for enhancement. PRK can also correct astigmatism (for example with slit, elliptical, scanning or mask techniques).

q.stem: How do radial keratotomy incisions reduce myopia?
options: Tissue is removed from the central cornea
The incisions lengthen the eye and reduce axial myopia
Intraocular pressure makes the weakened peripheral cornea bulge, flattening the centre
The incisions shrink the central collagen, steepening the cornea
q.explanation: Deep radial incisions in the mid-periphery and periphery weaken the cornea, so the intraocular pressure makes the wounds gape and the periphery bulge. Because the adult cornea does not stretch, the central cornea flattens, reducing its power. No tissue is removed and axial length is unchanged.

q.stem: How deep must radial keratotomy incisions be to have an effect?
q.explanation: Incisions need to reach about 80-90% of corneal thickness, which is why thickness is measured first with an ultrasound pachymeter and a diamond knife with adjustable footplates is used to limit the depth. Full thickness would perforate the eye.

q.stem: Which change would REDUCE the refractive effect of radial keratotomy?
q.explanation: Longer, deeper or more numerous incisions and a smaller central zone all increase the effect. A larger central zone lessens it; above about 5 mm there is little effect, while below 3 mm the incisions cause glare.

q.stem: What is a recognised long-term refractive change after radial keratotomy?
options: Stable refraction from the first postoperative week
A continuing hypermetropic shift of up to 1 D in a quarter or more of patients
Progressive myopic regression in most patients
q.explanation: Most eyes are stable after six months, but in at least a quarter a hypermetropic drift of up to 1.00 D continues over several years. Best results are in myopes under -5.00 D, where more than three-quarters finish within 1 D of emmetropia. The altered corneal shape can also make contact lens fitting difficult.

q.stem: What is the advantage of making four rather than eight radial incisions?
options: Further incisions can be added later for undercorrection, reducing overcorrection
Four incisions produce twice the effect of eight
Four incisions allow a smaller central zone
q.explanation: Four and eight incisions give comparable results, but starting with four leaves room to add more if the eye is undercorrected. This staged strategy may mean fewer patients end up overcorrected.

q.stem: Which method is best for correcting irregular astigmatism or high regular astigmatism that spectacles cannot manage?
options: Toric spectacle lenses with reduced cylinder
q.explanation: Spectacles do not adequately correct irregular or high regular astigmatism. A rigid contact lens creates a new regular front surface, and surgery is the alternative. Soft spherical lenses drape over the irregular cornea and do not neutralise it.

q.stem: After penetrating keratoplasty with interrupted sutures, keratometry shows the steepest meridian at 90. Which sutures should be removed selectively to reduce astigmatism?
q.explanation: Tight sutures steepen the cornea in their own meridian, so removing interrupted sutures in the steeper meridian lets it flatten. Removing sutures in the flatter meridian would increase the astigmatism. Topography-guided manipulation is more precise.

q.stem: A relaxing (transverse or arcuate) incision is placed in one meridian of the cornea. What is the effect on the corneal curvature?
options: Steepening in the meridian of the incision and flattening 90 degrees away
Flattening in the meridian of the incision and steepening 90 degrees away
No change until the sutures are removed
q.explanation: The cornea bulges at the incision, which flattens the central cornea in that meridian and increases curvature in the meridian at right angles. This is how relaxing incisions reduce astigmatism when placed in the steep meridian.

q.stem: Keratometry before cataract surgery reads 44.75 D at 180 and 43.25 D at 90. Where should a small-incision phaco wound be placed to help reduce the astigmatism?
q.explanation: The steeper meridian is 180 (44.75 D), giving 1.50 D of against-the-rule astigmatism. A small self-sealing incision flattens the cornea in its own meridian, so placing it in the steep meridian (temporal or nasal at 180) reduces the astigmatism. A superior wound would flatten the already flatter 90 meridian and increase it.

q.stem: Why is an arcuate relaxing incision theoretically preferable to a straight transverse one?
options: It always produces a larger correction
It avoids the need for a clear central zone
It lies in cornea of uniform thickness and is concentric with the visual axis
It is shorter and therefore heals faster
q.explanation: An arcuate cut stays at a constant distance from the visual axis and in cornea of uniform thickness, giving a more regular effect. A linear incision crosses cornea of varying thickness and parts of it lie closer to the axis. Longer incisions, or ones nearer the axis, have greater effect; nomograms relate zone diameter, arc length and number of incisions to the correction.

q.stem: Residual astigmatism persists after all corneal graft sutures have been removed. Where should relaxing incisions be placed for the most predictable effect?
options: Within the graft, in the steepest meridian
In the host cornea, in the flattest meridian
Across the graft-host junction in the flattest meridian
q.explanation: Incising the graft-host junction over 60-90 degrees where it is crossed by the steepest meridian reduces astigmatism, and placing the incisions wholly within the graft conserves the wound and is more predictable. Incisions in the flattest meridian would increase the astigmatism.

q.stem: A patient has more than 10 D of astigmatism after penetrating keratoplasty. Where is a wedge resection performed?
options: At the graft-host junction in the steepest meridian
At the graft-host junction in the flattest meridian
In the central graft along the visual axis
In the sclera behind the limbus
q.explanation: A deep arcuate wedge of 60-90 degrees is removed from the graft-host junction in the flattest meridian and closed with non-absorbable sutures. This shortens the cornea and steepens that meridian, the opposite of a relaxing incision, which is placed in the steepest meridian.

q.stem: How are compression sutures used to treat astigmatism after keratoplasty?
options: A tight suture across the junction in the flattest meridian steepens it
A loose suture in the flattest meridian flattens it
A tight suture across the junction in the steepest meridian steepens it further
Sutures are placed radially through the visual axis
q.explanation: A tight suture across the graft-host junction in the flattest meridian increases that meridian's curvature and reduces the astigmatism. The suture flattens the cornea immediately adjacent and pushes the apex away. For large errors, relaxing incisions can be combined with compression sutures placed 90 degrees away.

q.stem: Which statement about the intrastromal corneal ring is correct?
options: It requires ablation of the central cornea
It steepens the central cornea to treat hypermetropia
It flattens the central cornea to treat myopia up to about -4.00 D and is reversible
It is a permanent implant that cannot be removed
q.explanation: A PMMA split ring is inserted into a mid-peripheral stromal tunnel concentric with the limbus. It flattens the central curvature to treat myopia up to about -4.00 D without touching the central zone, and removing the ring reverses the effect.

q.stem: In keratomileusis, how is the removed lamella of anterior stroma reshaped, and which error can it correct?
options: On a cryolathe; high myopia but not hypermetropia
With an excimer laser in situ; hypermetropia only
With a diamond knife; low astigmatism
q.explanation: A microkeratome removes an anterior stromal lamella, which is reshaped on a cryolathe and replaced. High myopia, but not hypermetropia, can be corrected this way. Adding a donor lenticule to correct aphakia describes keratophakia.

q.stem: Keratophakia was developed as a modification of keratomileusis mainly to correct which condition?
q.explanation: In keratophakia an anterior stromal lamella is lifted and replaced over a shaped donor stromal lenticule to create a steeper corneal contour, which was intended to correct aphakia. Like keratomileusis it is technically difficult and unpredictable, so it has not been widely adopted.

q.stem: Which feature distinguishes epikeratophakia?
options: The eye is not entered and the lenticule can be removed to reverse it
A lamella of host stroma is removed and frozen
It is the preferred technique for correcting low myopia
It is performed with an excimer laser
q.explanation: A pre-shaped donor lenticule is attached to the surface of the host cornea, so the globe is not entered and the procedure is easily reversed by removing the lenticule. It is no longer used for myopia because outcomes were too variable.

q.stem: How does epikeratophakia for keratoconus differ from its use for myopia or hypermetropia?
options: A strongly minus-powered lenticule is placed loosely over the cone
A uniform-thickness lenticule is sutured tightly to compress the cone
The cone is excised before the lenticule is attached
A plus-powered lenticule is used to steepen the cornea
q.explanation: For keratoconus the lenticule is of uniform thickness and is sutured tightly so that it compresses the cone back towards a normal contour, neutralising the myopia. For myopia or hypermetropia, lenticules of different spherical power are used instead.

q.stem: In which situation might epikeratophakia still be useful today for aphakia?
options: In every case of aphakia, as first-line treatment
When the patient cannot tolerate contact lenses and an IOL is contraindicated
When a posterior chamber IOL is already present
q.explanation: Most aphakia is now corrected with a secondary intraocular lens. Epikeratophakia remains an option when contact lenses are not tolerated and an IOL is contraindicated.

q.stem: Which laser has replaced cautery for thermokeratoplasty, and what is its tissue effect?
options: Holmium:YAG; contraction of peripheral corneal collagen
q.explanation: Thermokeratoplasty uses focal low-temperature burns to make peripheral collagen contract and change corneal curvature; the Holmium:YAG laser has replaced cautery. It remains largely experimental. Excimer photoablation underlies PRK and LASIK.

q.stem: For which patients has clear lens extraction with IOL implantation been advocated?
q.explanation: The safety and predictability of small-incision cataract surgery led to removal of clear lenses to correct spherical errors, particularly in high myopia and in hypermetropes who are already presbyopic, who have little accommodation to lose.

q.stem: What is a claimed advantage of phakic intraocular lenses over corneal procedures, and what remains uncertain?
options: Accommodation is conserved; long-term effects on endothelium, lens and angle are unknown
They are fully reversible; their optical power is unpredictable
No intraocular surgery is needed; refractive stability is unknown
They correct only low errors; the risk of glare is unknown
q.explanation: Phakic IOLs in the anterior or posterior chamber are claimed to correct higher errors more predictably than corneal surgery while preserving accommodation, because the crystalline lens is kept. Their long-term effects on the corneal endothelium, crystalline lens and iridocorneal angle are not known.

q.stem: Which corneal incision is most likely to be astigmatically neutral?
options: A long incision in an elderly patient
A small incision far from the visual axis
A deep incision near the visual axis
A long incision close to the visual axis
q.explanation: Longer, deeper incisions or those nearer the visual axis have the greatest effect on central curvature, while small incisions further away are more neutral. Long incisions are also less stable and slower to heal, and healing is slower in the elderly, making outcomes less predictable.

q.stem: After extracapsular cataract surgery, one interrupted radial suture at 90 is tighter than the others. What astigmatic effect is expected?
q.explanation: A tight radial suture increases corneal curvature in its own meridian, producing with-the-rule astigmatism if at 90; a loose suture has the opposite effect. The suture can be cut once the wound has healed, and a continuous suture spreads tension more evenly.

q.stem: Why are temporal clear corneal phaco incisions relatively astigmatically neutral?
options: The temporal cornea has no collagen lamellae
The temporal limbus is further from the visual axis
q.explanation: The temporal limbus lies further from the visual axis than the superior limbus, so incisions there have less effect on central curvature. Surgeons who always operate temporally can manage pre-existing astigmatism with astigmatic keratotomies in the steeper axis.

q.stem: Why might the refraction change gradually for up to a year after sutured cataract surgery?
options: The intraocular lens slowly changes power
Degradation of the suture material reduces its tensile strength
q.explanation: As suture material degrades it loses tensile strength, so the corneal curvature it was holding changes gradually, for as long as a year after surgery. This is a corneal effect, not an IOL or axial length change.

q.stem: Which refractive tendency follows a penetrating keratoplasty in which the donor button is larger than the host trephination?
q.explanation: An oversized graft tends to be steeper and more powerful, so the eye is more likely to become myopic. Graft dimensions are one of the determinants of refractive outcome. Paediatric donor corneas, which are steeper and more powerful, can be useful in aphakic eyes.

q.stem: An aphakic eye needs penetrating keratoplasty. Why might a paediatric donor cornea be chosen?
options: It is flatter and reduces induced myopia
It has greater curvature and power, offsetting some aphakic hypermetropia
It has a thicker endothelium that resists rejection
q.explanation: Corneas from young donors are steeper and have greater refractive power, which helps counter the hypermetropia of aphakia. The other options are not the reasons given.

q.stem: An encircling scleral buckle increases the axial length of the eye by about 1 mm. What refractive change would be expected?
options: A myopic shift of about 0.3 D
A hypermetropic shift of about 3 D
A myopic shift of about 3 D
No change, as buckles affect only astigmatism
q.explanation: Indenting the globe with an encircling buckle lengthens the eye and induces myopia; each millimetre of axial length change corresponds to roughly 3 D. Asymmetric radial or segmental buckles also cause astigmatism, which reverses if the buckle is removed. A hypermetropic shift would follow shortening of the eye.

q.stem: What refractive change does silicone oil in the vitreous cavity of a phakic eye produce?
options: No change, as oil matches the vitreous index
A myopic shift of about -5 to -7 D
A hypermetropic shift of about +5 to +7 D
q.explanation: Behind the lens, silicone oil changes the convex posterior lens surface from a converging to a diverging interface, reducing the eye's total power and producing a hypermetropic shift of roughly +5 to +7 D. A myopic shift occurs instead in aphakic eyes, where the oil's convex anterior surface converges light.

q.stem: Why is the hypermetropia of an aphakic eye filled with silicone oil only about +4 to +6 D?
options: The oil causes the iris to act as a pinhole
The convex anterior oil surface acts as a converging lens, producing a myopic shift
The oil steepens the posterior cornea
The oil increases the axial length
q.explanation: In aphakia the oil bulges forward with a convex anterior surface, and its higher refractive index than aqueous makes this a converging interface. The resulting myopic shift partly offsets the aphakic hypermetropia. The oil does not change axial length or corneal curvature.

q.stem: A phakic eye has an intravitreal gas bubble. What is the effect on refraction?
options: A large hypermetropic shift because the lens becomes diverging
No change because gas has the same index as vitreous
A myopic shift caused by axial elongation
A large myopic shift because the posterior lens surface becomes strongly converging
q.explanation: Gas has a much lower refractive index than the lens, so the convex posterior lens surface becomes a powerful converging interface, causing a large myopic shift. This can allow indirect ophthalmoscopy without a condensing lens. In an aphakic gas-filled eye, the posterior corneal surface becomes strongly diverging and almost neutralises the cornea.
